title: From Randomness to Probability
text:
Learning Objectives
By the end of this session, you should be able to:

Define Random Phenomena and Probability.
Understand the Law of Large Numbers (LLN).
Apply the basic Rules of Probability (Addition, Multiplication, Complement).
Calculate probabilities for Disjoint and Independent events.

title: From Randomness to Probability
text:
1. Random Phenomena
A Random Phenomenon is a situation where we know what outcome could happen, but we don’t know which particular outcome will happen.

Example: Tossing a coin for “Tao o Ibon” (Heads or Tails).

We know it can be Tao or Ibon.
We don’t know which one it will be on the next toss.



Key Idea: Randomness is not chaos. It creates long-term patterns.

title: From Randomness to Probability
text:
Probability Definition
Probability is the long-run relative frequency of an event.
\[P(A) = \frac{\text{# of times A occurs}}{\text{Total # of trials}}\]

Subjective Probability: Personal belief (e.g., “I’m 90% sure it will rain”).
Empirical Probability: Based on data/observation.
Theoretical Probability: Based on a model (e.g., a fair die has 6 sides).

title: From Randomness to Probability
text:
2. The Law of Large Numbers (LLN)
Definition: As the number of independent trials increases, the long-run relative frequency of repeated events gets closer and closer to the true probability.

The Myth: “The Law of Averages” (Gambler’s Fallacy).

Scenario: You flip a coin 5 times, and get 5 Heads.
Fallacy: “Tails is due! It has to happen next.”
Truth: The coin has no memory. The probability is still 0.5.

title: From Randomness to Probability
text:
3. Probability Rules
Sample Space (\(S\))
The collection of all possible outcomes.

Example (1 Die): \(S = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\}\)

Rule 1: The Scale
A probability is a number between 0 and 1.
\[0 \le P(A) \le 1\]

\(P(A) = 0\): Impossible event.
\(P(A) = 1\): Certain event.

title: From Randomness to Probability
section: Rule 2: The “Something Has to Happen” Rule
text:
Rule 2: The “Something Has to Happen” Rule
The sum of probabilities of all possible outcomes must be 1.
\[P(S) = 1\]
Example: Board Exam
If there are only two outcomes: Pass or Fail. \[P(\text{Pass}) + P(\text{Fail}) = 100\% \text{ (or 1)}\]

title: From Randomness to Probability
text:
Rule 3: The Complement Rule
The probability of an event happening is 1 minus the probability that it does not happen.
\[P(A) = 1 - P(A^C)\]


 S  A \(A^C\)


Example: Rain
If \(P(\text{Rain}) = 0.20\), then \(P(\text{No Rain}) = 1 - 0.20 = 0.80\).

title: From Randomness to Probability
text:
Rule 4: The Addition Rule (Disjoint Events)
Two events are Disjoint (Mutually Exclusive) if they cannot happen at the same time.
\[P(A \text{ or } B) = P(A) + P(B)\]


 S  A  B Disjoint (No Overlap)


Example: Jeepney Colors

\(P(\text{Red}) = 0.3\), \(P(\text{Blue}) = 0.2\)
\(P(\text{Red or Blue}) = 0.3 + 0.2 = 0.5\)

title: From Randomness to Probability
text:
Rule 5: The Multiplication Rule (Independent Events)
Two events are Independent if the outcome of one does not influence the other.
\[P(A \text{ and } B) = P(A) \times P(B)\]
Example: Two Coin Flips
Getting “Tao” (Heads) on the first coin does not change the second coin.

\(P(\text{Tao}_1) = 0.5, P(\text{Tao}_2) = 0.5\)
\(P(\text{Tao}_1 \text{ and } \text{Tao}_2) = 0.5 \times 0.5 = 0.25\)

title: From Randomness to Probability
text:
Practice: “At Least One”
To calculate the probability of “At least one”, use the Complement Rule.
\[P(\text{At least one}) = 1 - P(\text{None})\]
Example: Defective Bulbs
Probability of a defective bulb is \(0.05\). You buy 3 bulbs. What is the chance at least one is defective?

Find \(P(\text{Good}) = 1 - 0.05 = 0.95\).
Find \(P(\text{3 Good}) = 0.95 \times 0.95 \times 0.95 = 0.857\) (assuming independence).
\(P(\text{At least one bad}) = 1 - 0.857 = 0.143\).

title: From Randomness to Probability
text:
Final Thought

“Statistics is never having to say you’re certain.”

We use probability to quantify uncertainty. It allows us to make rational decisions even when we cannot predict the exact future outcome.
